beats.intro: Some rules of arithmetic feel so natural that you use them without noticing. [[names]]In algebra we give them names, because they let us rearrange expressions with confidence. [[list]]This chapter covers three of them: [[c]]one about order, [[a]]one about grouping, [[d]]and one about sharing.
beats.commAdd: Start at zero. [[j3a]]Jump three, [[j5a]]then jump five. [[land1]]You land on eight. [[swap]]Now swap the order. [[j5b]]Jump five first, [[j3b]]then three. [[land2]]Eight again. [[def]]When you add, the order does not matter. [[name]]This is the commutative property of addition: [[rule]]a plus b equals b plus a.
beats.commMul: Multiplication works the same way. [[arr]]Here are three rows of five dots. Three times five is fifteen. [[turn]]Now give the picture a quarter turn. [[now]]It shows five rows of three: five times three. [[same]]No dot was added or taken away, so the answer is still fifteen. [[rule]]This is the commutative property of multiplication: x times y equals y times x. [[dot]]In algebra, a raised dot means times.
beats.commNot: But order does matter for subtraction and division. [[s1]]Seven minus two is five. [[s2]]Swap them, [[s2b]]and two minus seven is negative five. [[d1]]Eight divided by two is four, [[d2]]but two divided by eight [[d2b]]is one quarter. [[rule]]So the commutative property works only for addition and multiplication.
beats.q1: Quick check. Decide whether each statement is true or false.
beats.assocAdd: Now let's add three numbers: one, plus two, plus five. [[g1]]You could group the first two. [[g1a]]One plus two is three, [[g1b]]and three plus five is eight. [[g2]]Or you could group the last two. [[g2a]]Two plus five is seven, [[g2b]]and one plus seven is eight. [[same]]The grouping changed, but the sum did not. [[rule]]This is the associative property of addition. The parentheses can move, and the sum stays the same.
beats.assocMul: Grouping works for multiplication too. [[arr]]Here are two blocks, and each block has three rows of five dots. [[g1]]Group two times three first. [[g1a]]That makes six rows of five, [[g1b]]which is thirty dots. [[g2]]Or group three times five first. [[g2a]]Each block holds fifteen dots, [[g2b]]and two blocks make thirty. [[rule]]This is the associative property of multiplication.
beats.assocNot: Like the commutative property, this one works only for addition and multiplication. [[s1]]Eight minus four is four, and four minus two is two. [[s2]]But if you group the four and the two first, four minus two is two, and eight minus two is six. [[diff]]Two is not six, so grouping matters for subtraction.
beats.orderGroup: So what's the difference between the two? [[c]]Commutative is about order. [[cs]]The numbers trade places. [[a]]Associative is about grouping. [[as]]The numbers stay where they are, and only the parentheses move.
beats.q2: Quick check. Two questions about order and grouping.
beats.distIntro: The third property mixes multiplication with addition. [[q]]What is three times the sum of six and eight? [[whole]]Picture a rectangle three squares tall and fourteen squares wide. That's forty-two squares. [[split]]Now split it where the six meets the eight. [[p1]]The left part is three times six, eighteen. [[p2]]The right part is three times eight, twenty-four. [[sum]]Eighteen plus twenty-four is forty-two, the same as before. [[share]]The three was shared with both the six and the eight. [[name]]This is the distributive property.
beats.distLetters: In general, for any numbers a, b, and c, [[rule]]a times the sum of b and c equals a b plus a c. [[ab]]Two letters side by side, like a b, mean a times b. [[pic]]The rectangle shows why. [[h]]Its height is a, [[w]]and its width is b plus c. [[parts]]So its area is a b plus a c.
beats.distSub: It works with subtraction as well. [[q]]Take two times the difference of ten and seven. [[big]]Start with a rectangle two squares tall and ten wide: twenty squares. [[cut]]Take away a piece two tall and seven wide: fourteen squares. [[left]]Six squares remain. [[check]]And that matches: ten minus seven is three, and two times three is six. [[rule]]So a times the difference of b and c equals a b minus a c.
beats.q3: Quick check. Use the distributive property, and fill in the missing numbers.
beats.distMulti: The same idea works with more terms inside the parentheses. [[q]]Take six times two, minus one, plus five, all in parentheses. [[a1]]Share the six with every term. Six times two, [[a2]]minus six times one, [[a3]]plus six times five. [[calc]]That's twelve, minus six, plus thirty, [[res]]which is thirty-six. [[check]]Check: two minus one plus five is six, and six times six is thirty-six.
beats.distNotDiv: One warning. [[div]]A number divided by a sum cannot be split this way. [[left]]Forty divided by the sum of eight and two is forty divided by ten, which is four. [[right]]But forty divided by eight, plus forty divided by two, is five plus twenty, which is twenty-five. [[diff]]Four is not twenty-five.
beats.q4: Quick check. Which statement is true?
beats.wrap: Three properties to remember. [[c]]Commutative: you can change the order of numbers you add or multiply. [[a]]Associative: you can change how they are grouped. [[d]]Distributive: a number that multiplies a sum is shared with every term. [[warn]]Subtraction and division don't follow the first two, so check before you swap or regroup. [[end]]Now try the chapter practice.
